For $n,d\ge1$, a deterministic design $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, response $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and penalty $\tau>0$, define the Lasso objective
$$Q_y(\theta)=\frac1n\|y-X\theta\|_2^2+2\tau\|\theta\|_1.$$
Its minimizer set is $\mathcal M(y)=\operatorname{argmin}_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}Q_y(\theta)$. The penalty is strictly positive; no full-rank condition on $X$ is imposed. The nonemptiness, compactness, and convexity of this set are proved separately; this page defines the objective and minimizer set but does not select one minimizer.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

derivations.claim: The function $Q_y$ is continuous. For $0\le t\le1$, the identity $\|ta+(1-t)b\|_2^2=t\|a\|_2^2+(1-t)\|b\|_2^2-t(1-t)\|a-b\|_2^2$ proves convexity of the squared-residual term, while $|tu+(1-t)v|\le t|u|+(1-t)|v|$ in each coordinate proves convexity of $\|\cdot\|_1$. Since $\|\theta\|_1=\sum_j|\theta_j|\ge\|\theta\|_2$ (squaring both sides reduces this to nonnegative cross terms $2|\theta_j||\theta_k|$), $Q_y(\theta)\ge2\tau\|\theta\|_2\to\infty$ as $\|\theta\|_2\to\infty$. Choose $R>0$ with $2\tau R>Q_y(0)$. By [F2], $Q_y$ attains a minimum on the closed radius-$R$ ball; every point outside that ball has objective greater than $Q_y(0)$, so a global minimum is attained inside the ball.

The minimizer set is closed as the inverse image $Q_y^{-1}(\{\min Q_y\})$ of a closed singleton under a continuous function, and it is contained in the closed radius-$R$ ball from step 1.1. Hence it is compact by [F2]. If $\theta_1,\theta_2$ are minimizers and $0\le t\le1$, convexity gives $Q_y(t\theta_1+(1-t)\theta_2)\le tQ_y(\theta_1)+(1-t)Q_y(\theta_2)=\min Q_y$; by minimality equality holds, so the minimizer set is convex.

$$\mathcal C(S)=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:\|v_{S^c}\|_1\le3\|v_S\|_1\}.$$

$$\frac{\|Xv\|_2^2}{n}\ge\kappa^2\|v_S\|_2^2$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

Let $U,V$ be centered real random variables, not necessarily independent, each sub-Gaussian with proxy $K^2>0$ as in [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]]. Then $W=UV-\mathbb E[UV]$ is sub-exponential with parameters $(256K^4,16K^2)$ under the restricted-MGF convention of that definition.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered real random variables, with $X_i$ sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu_i^2,b_i)$ as defined in [[def-subgaussian-variable-and-vector]], where $n\ge1$ and $b_i>0$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\nu_i^2$, $b=\max_{1\le i\le n}b_i$, and $S=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac12\min\!\left\{\frac{t^2}{v},\frac{t}{b}\right\}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric and let $\mathcal N$ be a $1/4$-net of the Euclidean unit sphere in $\mathbb R^p$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2\max_{v\in\mathcal N}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|.$$
The operator norm is the finite-dimensional norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

Let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ be centered sub-Gaussian real random variables with a common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$, where $m\ge1$. No independence is assumed. For $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le j\le m}|Y_j|\ge t\right)\le2m\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ the probability is $0$.

Let $Z$ be a centered sub-Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^d$ with proxy $\sigma^2$, where $d\ge1$. For $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N$ be the sphere net supplied by [[lem-epsilon-net-of-unit-sphere-has-cardinality-bound]]. Then for $t>0$, if $\sigma^2>0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|Z\|_2\ge t)\le2(1+2/\epsilon)^d\exp\!\left(-\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),$$
and if $\sigma^2=0$ this probability is $0$. The deterministic reduction is $\|z\|_2\le(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\max_{u\in\mathcal N}|\langle u,z\rangle|$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

derivations.claim: If $L=0$, [F2] and [F6] imply $P(\|Z_i\|_2\ge1/m)=0$ for each $i$ and positive integer $m$. By [F8], the countable union over $i,m$ shows that every $Z_i=0$ almost surely; then [F9] gives $\Sigma=0$, and both estimators are exact. Assume $L>0$. Fix a unit vector $u$ and set $W_i=(u^{\mathsf T}Z_i)^2-E[(u^{\mathsf T}Z_i)^2]$. By [F2]–[F3], each $W_i$ is centered sub-exponential with parameters $(256L^2,16L)$; [F10] gives that these variables are iid across $i$.

By [F10] the sample vectors are independent, and [F7] gives, for every $u\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, $E e^{\lambda\langle u,\bar Z\rangle}=\prod_{i=1}^n E e^{(\lambda/n)\langle u,Z_i\rangle}\le e^{L\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/(2n)}.$ Thus $\bar Z$ is centered sub-Gaussian with proxy $L/n$. Applying the vector clause of [F6] with a $1/2$-net at $s=4\sqrt{Lr}$ gives $P(\|\bar Z\|_2^2>16Lr)\le2\cdot5^p e^{-2(p+x)}\le\delta/2,$ since $r=(p+x)/n$ and $x=\log(4/\delta)$.

Applying [F4] to $\sum_iW_i$ gives, for every $t>0$, $P\left(\left|u^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma)u\right|>t\right)\le2\exp\left[-\frac12\min\left\{\frac{nt^2}{256L^2},\frac{nt}{16L}\right\}\right].$ This is uniform over unit $u$.

Take a $1/4$-net with at most $9^p$ points and put $x=\log(4/\delta)$, so $r=(p+x)/n$. With $C_0=80$ and $t=C_0L(\sqrt r+r)$, the exponent in step 2.1 is at least $\frac12\min\{80^2/256,80/16\}(p+x)=\frac52(p+x)\ge p\log9+x$. A union bound gives probability at least $1-\delta/2$ that every net quadratic form is at most $t$ in absolute value.
By [F9], $\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma$ is symmetric. On the event in step 3.1, [F5] gives $\|\widehat\Sigma_0-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2t=160L(\sqrt r+r)$. This proves the first estimate.

Expanding [F1] gives $\widehat\Sigma^*=\widehat\Sigma_0-\bar Z\bar Z^{\mathsf T}$. For $w\ne0$ and unit $v$, [F12] gives $\|ww^{\mathsf T}v\|_2=\|w\|_2|\langle w,v\rangle|\le\|w\|_2^2$, with equality at $v=w/\|w\|_2$; if $w=0$, both sides vanish. Thus [F11] gives $\|\bar Z\bar Z^{\mathsf T}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\bar Z\|_2^2$. For vectors $a,b$, [F12] and $\|a+b\|_2^2=\|a\|_2^2+2\langle a,b\rangle+\|b\|_2^2$ give $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2$; applying this inside the maximum in [F11] gives $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Combining the probability-$1-\delta/2$ events from steps 1.2 and 3.1, their intersection has probability at least $1-\delta$ by [F8], and the resulting error is at most $160L(\sqrt r+r)+16Lr\le176L(\sqrt r+r)$.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Input: observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, with integers $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and a fixed threshold constant $\gamma_\tau>0$ determined by the directional sub-Gaussian tail parameter $\tau$.

Compute the sample-centered covariance $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]] and put $\lambda=\gamma_\tau\sqrt{\log(p)/n}$. Output the symmetric matrix $\widehat\Sigma$ defined by
$$\widehat\sigma_{jj}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jj},\qquad \widehat\sigma_{jk}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}\mathbf 1\{|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|\ge\lambda\}\quad(j\ne k).$$
The diagonal is unchanged; an off-diagonal entry at threshold equality is retained. This procedure is a definition and makes no risk or positive-semidefiniteness guarantee.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, where $p\ge1$. Then
$$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_{\|v\|_2=1}|v^{\mathsf T}Av|=\max_j|\lambda_j|,$$
where $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

derivations.claim: On the event in the Statement, each diagonal error is at most $\lambda/2$. For an off-diagonal entry that is retained, $|\sigma_{jk}|\ge\lambda/2$ and $|\widehat\sigma_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|\le\lambda/2\le\min\{|\sigma_{jk}|,\lambda\}$. If it is removed, then $|\sigma_{jk}|\le|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|+|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|<3\lambda/2$, and its error is $|\sigma_{jk}|\le(3/2)\min\{|\sigma_{jk}|,\lambda\}$.

For $q=0$, [F1] and step 1.1 bound every off-diagonal column error sum by $(3/2)c_{n,p}\lambda$. For $0<q<1$, fix a column, put $a_k=|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}$, $T=c_{n,p}\lambda^{-q}$, and $B_q:=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}2^{r(1-1/q)}=\frac1{1-2^{1-1/q}}<\infty.$ The class bound in [F1] gives $a_k\le(c_{n,p}/k)^{1/q}$. If $T<1$, then $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\min(a_k,\lambda)\le c_{n,p}^{1/q}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-1/q}\le B_qc_{n,p}^{1/q}\le B_qc_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q},$ because grouping $2^r\le k<2^{r+1}$ gives at most $2^r(2^r)^{-1/q}$ per block, and $c_{n,p}<\lambda^q$. If $T\ge1$, let $m=\lfloor T\rfloor\ge T/2$. The first $m$ terms contribute at most $m\lambda\le c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$. Grouping the tail into blocks $2^rm<k\le2^{r+1}m$ gives $\sum_{k>m}k^{-1/q}\le B_qm^{1-1/q},$ so the tail contributes at most $B_qc_{n,p}^{1/q}m^{1-1/q}\le B_q2^{1/q-1}c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$; here the exponent $1-1/q$ is negative and $m\ge T/2$. Thus for either case each off-diagonal column error sum is at most $C_qc_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}$ for a finite constant $C_q$ depending only on $q$. Adding the diagonal error bound $\lambda/2$ from step 1.1 bounds every row sum by $C_q(c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}+\lambda)$. For $q=0$, the same total is at most $(3/2)c_{n,p}\lambda+\lambda/2\le2(c_{n,p}\lambda+\lambda)$.

For any unit vector $v$, [F3] identifies the operator norm with the maximum absolute Rayleigh quotient. With $A=\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma$, symmetry and $2|v_jv_k|\le v_j^2+v_k^2$ give $|v^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma)v| \le\sum_{j,k}|A_{jk}||v_j||v_k| \le\frac12\sum_{j,k}|A_{jk}|(v_j^2+v_k^2) \le\max_j\sum_k|A_{jk}|,$ because $A$ is symmetric, its absolute column sums equal its row sums, and $\sum_jv_j^2=1$. Taking the maximum over unit $v$ and using step 2.1 yields the claimed operator bound.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

derivations.claim: The tail bound and [F1] imply $\mathbb E e^{a|X|}=1+a\int_0^\infty e^{at}\mathbb P(|X|>t)\,dt\le1+2a\int_0^\infty e^{at-t^2/(2\tau)}\,dt<\infty$ for every $a>0$, since completing the square gives $at-t^2/(2\tau)=-(t-a\tau)^2/(2\tau)+a^2\tau/2$. Thus all MGFs below are finite.

Let $X_1,X_2$ be the coordinate variables on the product of two copies of the law of $X$; [F2] gives this probability space, and its rectangle formula makes them independent with law equal to that of $X$. Set $D=X_1-X_2$. Independence [F3] gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda D}=(\mathbb E e^{\lambda X})(\mathbb E e^{-\lambda X})$. $$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if

$$

and if $v=0$ then $\mathbb P(|S|\ge t)=0$.

2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable

  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$

$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.

   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

The matrices have the same $p$-dimensional domain; [F2] and this nullspace inclusion give $\operatorname{rank}(C^{\mathsf T}C)\le\operatorname{rank}(C)\le n-1<p$. Multiplication by $1/n\ne0$ does not change rank, so $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ is singular.

citations.quote: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Let $\mathcal Q$ be a family of probability laws on a common measurable sample space $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)$, and let $\Sigma(Q)\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be a specified matrix parameter for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, with fixed $p\ge1$. Give $\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ its usual Euclidean topology and Borel sigma-algebra. An estimator is a measurable map $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal Z,\mathcal C)\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$. Define its squared operator risk at $Q$ and the minimax risk over $\mathcal Q$ by
$$R_Q(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_Q\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(Q)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R(\mathcal Q)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{Q\in\mathcal Q}R_Q(\widehat\Sigma).$$

For a family $\mathcal P$ of one-observation laws on a common measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and an integer $n\ge1$, the $n$-observation experiment observes $n$ independent observations, each with law $P$. Its sample space is $(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})$ and its sample law is the finite product probability measure $P^{\otimes n}$; this is the joint law of the IID family in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[def-independent-random-elements]]. For estimators $\widehat\Sigma:(\mathcal X^n,\mathcal A^{\otimes n})\to(\mathbb R^{p\times p},\mathcal B(\mathbb R^{p\times p}))$, define
$$R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma)=\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(P)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2,\qquad\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal P)=\inf_{\widehat\Sigma}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_{n,P}(\widehat\Sigma).$$

An infinite expectation is allowed, so every measurable estimator has an extended nonnegative risk. Suprema of risks are taken in the ordered range $[0,\infty]$, with $\sup\varnothing:=0$, its least element. Thus when $\mathcal Q$ or $\mathcal P$ is empty the corresponding supremum is zero for every estimator, and its minimax risk is zero. The estimator class is nonempty because the constant zero matrix map is measurable. The operator norm is from [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition ([[def-metric-ball]]).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $m\ge1$, let U,V be open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, and let $T:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_V h(y)\,dy=\int_U h(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$, with equality in $[0,\infty]$ and $0\cdot\infty=0$. This statement concerns Borel h; no completed-measurable substitution is asserted.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: Choose $v^2<(\beta-1)/(4\beta)$ and put $r=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$. Write $x=c/[2(s\epsilon)^q]$, so $x\ge2$ and $k=\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2\ge2$. The radius condition gives $x\le C\sqrt n/(\log p)^{3/2}$, hence $k^2\le Cn/(\log p)^3$, $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, and $n\epsilon^4k^2\le C/\log p$. Also $k^2p^{2v^2}/r\le Cp^{1/\beta+2v^2-1}/(\log p)^3\to0$, uniformly over admitted $n,c$. All constants depend only on fixed parameters. Increase $P_0$ so $r\ge16k$, $2k\epsilon\le1/3$, and the small bounds below hold. Let $\Lambda$ be all $r\times r$ zero-one matrices with every row sum $k$ and every column sum at most $2k$; cyclic shifts of a $k$-set show it is nonempty. For $\gamma\in\{0,1\}^r$, embed $D_\gamma\lambda$ as the upper-right block of a symmetric off-diagonal matrix $A(\gamma,\lambda)$, using two disjoint $r$-coordinate blocks and an extra zero coordinate if $p$ is odd, and put $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}=s(I_p+\epsilon A(\gamma,\lambda))$. Every absolute row sum of $A$ is at most $2k$. For any $z$, $|z^{\mathsf T}Az|\le\frac12\sum_{j,l}|A_{jl}|(z_j^2+z_l^2)\le2k\|z\|_2^2$; applying this to unit eigenvectors and using [F4] bounds the eigenvalues of $A$ in $[-2k,2k]$. Thus $\Sigma_{\gamma,\lambda}$ is positive definite with eigenvalues in $[2s/3,4s/3]\subset(0,\tau]$. Each column has at most $2k$ off-diagonal entries of magnitude $s\epsilon$. If $0<q<1$, its weak-$\ell_q$ quantity is at most $2k(s\epsilon)^q\le c$; if $q=0$, its nonzero count is at most $2k\le c$. Hence [F2] puts every covariance in the radius-$c$ class. The standard-normal density gives $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}\,dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$, so [F1] verifies the directional-tail condition. For any rectangular matrix $M$ and vector $z$, [F5] gives $|(Mz)_i|^2\le(\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\sum_j|M_{ij}|z_j^2)$. Summing over rows yields $\|Mz\|_2^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)\|z\|_2^2$, hence $\|M\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le(\max_i\sum_j|M_{ij}|)(\max_j\sum_i|M_{ij}|)$. Therefore each cross-block matrix $C=\epsilon D_{\gamma_{-1}}L$ below has $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sqrt2k\epsilon\le2k\epsilon$.

Give $(\gamma,\lambda)$ the uniform prior on $\{0,1\}^r\times\Lambda$. Fix bit $i$, say $i=1$ by row symmetry, and condition on the remaining bit vector $\gamma_{-1}$ and nuisance rows $L=(\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_r)$. The number of possible first-row supports is $N(L)=\binom{d(L)}k$, where $d(L)$ counts columns whose nuisance sum is less than $2k$. Since there are $(r-1)k$ nuisance ones, $d(L)\ge r/2$. The marginal prior of $L$ is $\pi(L)=N(L)/|\Lambda|$, independent of $\gamma_{-1}$; conditional on $L$, a support $A$ is uniform among its $N(L)$ available $k$-sets. For each fixed $\gamma_{-1}$, when $\gamma_1=0$ let $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ be the Gaussian n-sample law, which does not depend on $A$; when $\gamma_1=1$, let $P_{\gamma_{-1},A,L}$ be the n-sample law and $\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}$ its uniform support mixture. In the chi-square expansion draw two independent available supports $A,B$ given $L$. Their joint mass with $L$ is proportional to $1/N(L)$, so given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ the nuisance rows are not asserted uniform.

Fix $\gamma_{-1}$ and let $C\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ be the cross-block matrix with first row zero and remaining rows $\epsilon\gamma_l\lambda_l$. Under $Q_{\gamma_{-1},L}$, after canceling $s$, the covariance is $B_0=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&I_r\end{pmatrix}$, with an extra identity coordinate if $p$ is odd. Put $R=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{1/2}$; it is positive definite because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$. The block matrix $T=\begin{pmatrix}I_r&0\\C^{\mathsf T}&R\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $TT^{\mathsf T}=B_0$. Whiten by $T^{-1}$, extended by the identity on any extra coordinate. If $e=e_1$ is the first coordinate in the left block and $v_A=\mathbf1_A$ is the right-block support vector, then $T^{-1}e=e$ and $T^{-1}v_A=R^{-1}v_A$. Thus the alternative covariances become $I+\Delta_A$ and $I+\Delta_B$, where $\Delta_A=eu^{\mathsf T}+ue^{\mathsf T}$, $\Delta_B=ew^{\mathsf T}+we^{\mathsf T}$, $u=\epsilon R^{-1}v_A$, $w=\epsilon R^{-1}v_B$, and $u,w\perp e$. With $H=(I_r-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}$, $u^{\mathsf T}w=t=\epsilon^2\mathbf1_A^{\mathsf T}H\mathbf1_B$. The operator norms of $\Delta_A,\Delta_B$ equal $\|u\|_2,\|w\|_2$, respectively. Since $\|R^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1/2}$, these norms are at most $\epsilon\sqrt{k}/\sqrt{1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2}<1/4$ for large $P_0$; here $\epsilon\sqrt{k}=(k\epsilon)/\sqrt{k}\le C/(\sqrt2\log p)$. For positive-definite $S$, [F1], [F6] and [F7] give the Lebesgue density $f_S(x)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det S)^{-1/2}\exp(-x^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}x/2)$: the independent standard-normal coordinates have product density, and the invertible linear map $S^{1/2}$ changes variables with determinant $(\det S)^{1/2}$. For the one-observation laws, write $f_A,f_B,f_0$ for the positive densities of the two alternatives and the whitened baseline. Put $M=(I+\Delta_A)^{-1}+(I+\Delta_B)^{-1}-I$. Each inverse has smallest eigenvalue at least $(1+1/4)^{-1}=4/5$, hence $M\succeq(3/5)I$. The product density $f_Af_B/f_0$ has exponent matrix $M$ and normalizing factor $(2\pi)^{-p/2}[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)]^{-1/2}$. Diagonalizing $M$ by [F4], applying an orthogonal change of variables and scaling each one-dimensional standard-normal density [F6, F7] gives $$\int \frac{f_A(x)f_B(x)}{f_0(x)}\,dx=[\det(I+\Delta_A)\det(I+\Delta_B)\det M]^{-1/2}.$$ The identity $(I+\Delta_A)M(I+\Delta_B)=I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ and determinant multiplicativity [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]] reduce it to $\det(I-\Delta_A\Delta_B)^{-1/2}$. Since $u,w\perp e$, $\Delta_A\Delta_B=tee^{\mathsf T}+uw^{\mathsf T}$. On $\operatorname{span}\{e\}$, $I-\Delta_A\Delta_B$ contributes determinant $1-t$. On $e^\perp$, if $u=0$ the rank-one determinant is $1$; otherwise choose an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u/\|u\|_2$, so $I-uw^{\mathsf T}$ has only its first row changed and determinant $1-w^{\mathsf T}u=1-t$. The full determinant is $(1-t)^2$, and the one-observation cross integral is $(1-t)^{-1}$. The n-sample laws have product densities by the product joint-law supplier in [F6]; repeated Tonelli [F8] therefore makes their cross integral the nth power, $(1-t)^{-n}$.

Write $J=|A\cap B|$, $X_l=|A\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$ and $Y_l=|B\cap\operatorname{supp}\lambda_l|$. The identity $H-I=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}C$ follows from $H-I=(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)^{-1}C^{\mathsf T}C$ and $(I-C^{\mathsf T}C)C^{\mathsf T}=C^{\mathsf T}(I-CC^{\mathsf T})$. The Neumann series $(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}=\sum_{m\ge0}(CC^{\mathsf T})^m$ converges because $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$; since $C$ has nonnegative entries, $H-I$ is entrywise nonnegative and $t-J\epsilon^2\ge0$. The eigenvalues of $CC^{\mathsf T}$ lie in $[0,\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2]$, so [F4] gives $\|(I-CC^{\mathsf T})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$. Also $(C\mathbf1_A)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lX_l$ and $(C\mathbf1_B)_l=\epsilon\gamma_lY_l$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ yield $$0\le t-J\epsilon^2\le\frac{\epsilon^4}{2(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)}\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2).$$ Since $\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)^{-1}$ and $\|\mathbf1_A\|_2=\|\mathbf1_B\|_2=\sqrt{k}$, [F5] also gives $t\le\epsilon^2k/(1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$. Since $k\ge2$ and $k\epsilon\le C/\log p$, $\epsilon^2k=(k\epsilon)^2/k=o(1)$, so $t=o(1)$. The derivative of $-\log(1-x)$ is at most $2$ for $0\le x\le t\le1/2$; since $1-\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge8/9$, the preceding bound gives $$(1-t)^{-n}\le(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\exp\left\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\right\},\qquad\theta=2n\epsilon^4.$$

Fix $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ and all nuisance rows except row $l$, and let $a_j$ be the sum in column $j$ over those fixed rows. A support $S$ for row $l$ is feasible exactly when $|S|=k$, $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}\le2k$ for every column, and $a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k$ for every $j\in A\cup B$ (so both first-row supports remain available). Thus before prior weighting row $l$ is uniform over the $k$-subsets of the fixed set $$V=\{j\in A\cup B:a_j\le2k-2\}\cup\{j\notin A\cup B:a_j\le2k-1\}.$$ At most $(r-2)k/(2k)\le r/2$ columns outside $A\cup B$ have $a_j=2k$, so deleting these and $A\cup B$ leaves at least $r/2-2k\ge r/4$ available columns; hence $d_0=|V|\ge r/4$. The first-row availability count is $d(L)=\#\{j:a_j+\mathbf1_{\{j\in S\}}<2k\}$; as $S$ varies, only columns outside $A\cup B$ with $a_j=2k-1$ can change this count, so its range has width at most $k\le2k$. Since $d(L)\ge r/2$ and $\binom{d+1}k/\binom dk=(d+1)/(d+1-k)$, the ratio of any two weights $1/N(L)$ is at most $\exp(Ck^2/r)\le2$ after increasing $P_0$. Thus the actual conditional density of the row support is at most twice the uniform-subset density on $V$. If $m=|A\cap V|$, singleton and ordered-pair inclusion probabilities give $E X_l=mk/d_0\le Ck^2/r$ and $E[X_l(X_l-1)]=m(m-1)k(k-1)/(d_0(d_0-1))\le Ck^4/r^2$. Hence $E X_l^2\le C(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$; the same bound holds for $Y_l$ and under the weighted law with twice the constant. Since $\theta k^2=o(1)$, $e^z-1\le2z$ for $0\le z\le1$ yields $$E[\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid\text{all other rows},A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2).$$

Put $f_l=\exp\{\theta(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}$ and $B_0=1+C\theta(k^2/r+k^4/r^2)$. Every factor except $f_l$ is measurable when all rows except $l$ are fixed. Thus for any subset $S$ containing $l$, conditional expectation gives $$E[\prod_{j\in S}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0 E[\prod_{j\in S\setminus\{l\}}f_j\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}].$$ Iterating over the finitely many nuisance rows yields $$E[\exp\{\theta\sum_{l=2}^r(X_l^2+Y_l^2)\}\mid A,B,\gamma_{-1}]\le B_0^{r-1}\le\exp\{Cn\epsilon^4(k^2+k^4/r)\}=1+o(1)$$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. No row independence is used.

Given $L$, $A,B$ are independent uniform $k$-subsets of a set of size $d\ge r/2$. Expanding $z^J=(1+(z-1))^J$ and using $$E\binom Jj=\binom kj\frac{(k)_j}{(d)_j}\le\frac{[k^2/(d-k+1)]^j}{j!}$$ gives $E[z^J\mid L]\le\exp\{k^2(z-1)/(d-k+1)\}$. Since $J\le k$ and $\epsilon^2k=o(1)$, $(1-J\epsilon^2)^{-n}\le\exp(2n\epsilon^2J)=p^{2v^2J}$. Define $\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=\int(d\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L}/dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}-1)^2\,dQ_{\gamma_{-1},L}$. Finite expansion of the mixture density gives $$1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})=E_{A,B\mid L,\gamma_{-1}}(1-t)^{-n}.$$ The posterior of $L$ given $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$ has weights proportional to $1/N(L)$; step 6.1 bounds the conditional remainder factor by $1+o(1)$ uniformly in $A,B,\gamma_{-1}$. Since $d-k+1\ge r/3$, the overlap generating-function bound is uniform in $L,\gamma_{-1}$ and yields $$E_{\gamma_{-1},L}[1+\chi^2(\overline P_{\gamma_{-1},L},Q_{\gamma_{-1},L})]\le(1+o(1))\exp(Ck^2p^{2v^2}/r)=1+o(1),$$ using step 1.1. For each fixed $(\gamma_{-1},L)$, if $R=d\overline P/dQ$, then $E_Q(R-1)=0$, so the positive and negative parts of $R-1$ have equal integrals, and the event $\{R\ge1\}$ attains the supremum in [F9]; hence $\operatorname{TV}(\overline P,Q)=\tfrac12E_Q|R-1|$; [F10] bounds this by $\tfrac12\sqrt{\chi^2(\overline P,Q)}$. Finite Cauchy--Schwarz [F5] over the common prior weights on $(\gamma_{-1},L)$ bounds the average conditional total variation by $\tfrac12\sqrt{E_{\gamma_{-1},L}\chi^2}$, at most $1/2$ after increasing $P_0$. The same mixing weights are used under bit $i=0$ and bit $i=1$, so the full sample-law mixtures have total variation at most $1/2$ by the triangle inequality for the density integral. Their density affinity satisfies $$\int\min(dP_{i,0},dP_{i,1})=1-\operatorname{TV}(P_{i,0},P_{i,1})\ge1/2.$$

For parameters with $h$ different bits, apply their covariance difference to the vector that is one on the right block and zero elsewhere. Each changed bit contributes a distinct left-block coordinate of magnitude $s\epsilon k$, independently of support choices, so the squared output norm is at least $h(s\epsilon k)^2$ while the input squared norm is $r$. Hence $\|\Sigma_\theta-\Sigma_{\theta'}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\ge h(s\epsilon k)^2/r$. Given any measurable matrix estimator, choose a nearest finite covariance target with a fixed tie order. The finite distance comparisons are measurable: [F5] bounds the operator norm by the Frobenius norm, and its triangle inequality follows by applying the Euclidean triangle inequality to every unit vector, so distance to each fixed target is continuous. A wrong target decision forces squared estimation loss at least one quarter of the squared target separation. For each bit, the sum of its two conditional testing errors is at least the density affinity, since pointwise the test contributes at least the minimum of the two densities. By step 7.1, under the uniform prior each bit error probability is at least $1/4$, so the average number of bit errors is at least $r/4$. The maximal risk is at least the average risk and therefore at least $(s\epsilon k)^2/16$. Finally, $k\ge c/[4(s\epsilon)^q]$ implies this is at least $b c^2a^{1-q}$ for a positive constant depending only on the fixed parameters.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ of [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], with $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and $\tau>0$. Let $u>0$ and let $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ be the sample-centered covariance. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}| \le192\tau\left(\sqrt{\frac un}+\frac un\right)\right)\ge1-2pe^{-u}-2p^2e^{-2u}.$$
In particular $u=\log(8p^4)$ gives the original probability $1-p^{-2}$.
No independence between coordinates of a single observation is assumed.

Let $\Sigma\in G_q(c_{n,p})$ from [[def-weak-lq-sparse-covariance-class]], let $\widehat\Sigma$ be the output of [[alg-entrywise-thresholded-sample-covariance]] with threshold $\lambda>0$, and suppose
$$\max_{1\le j,k\le p}|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|\le\lambda/2.$$
Then
$$\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_q\left(c_{n,p}\lambda^{1-q}+\lambda\right),$$
where $C_q<\infty$ depends only on $q$; for $q=0$, the class means at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries per column and one may take $C_0=2$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb R^p$ with finite second moments, mean $\mu=\mathbb E X_1$, and covariance matrix
$$\Sigma=\mathbb E[(X_1-\mu)(X_1-\mu)^{\mathsf T}].$$
The oracle-centered sample covariance and the sample-centered covariance are respectively
$$\widehat\Sigma_\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)(X_i-\mu)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat\Sigma^\ast=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T},\quad \bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
For a matrix estimate $A$, squared operator loss is $\|A-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$, with the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. This definition distinguishes the known-mean raw second moment from the estimator that removes an unknown mean.

Input: observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^p$, with integers $n\ge1$, $p\ge2$, and a fixed threshold constant $\gamma_\tau>0$ determined by the directional sub-Gaussian tail parameter $\tau$.

Compute the sample-centered covariance $\widehat\Sigma^\ast$ from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]] and put $\lambda=\gamma_\tau\sqrt{\log(p)/n}$. Output the symmetric matrix $\widehat\Sigma$ defined by
$$\widehat\sigma_{jj}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jj},\qquad \widehat\sigma_{jk}=\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}\mathbf 1\{|\widehat\sigma^\ast_{jk}|\ge\lambda\}\quad(j\ne k).$$
The diagonal is unchanged; an off-diagonal entry at threshold equality is retained. This procedure is a definition and makes no risk or positive-semidefiniteness guarantee.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then

$$\Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big)^{2} \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}\Big)\Big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}\Big),$$

and, in root form ([[thm-of-square-roots]]),

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\Big| \;\le\; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} a_k^{2}} \; \sqrt{\sum_{k<n} b_k^{2}}.$$

Equality holds in the first display if and only if the two lists are
proportional, in the symmetric sense that there is a pair
$(\lambda, \mu) \ne (0,0)$ of reals with $\lambda a_k = \mu b_k$ for every
$k < n$.

**No root is used in the proof of the squared form.** That form is an identity
plus a sign argument in the ordered field, and the root form is only a
restatement of it through the monotonicity of squaring on the nonnegatives
([[lem-of-square-monotone]]); the root enters nowhere but the last step, where
that restatement is made and [[thm-of-square-roots]] is what supplies the
square-root symbol. This matters here, because it makes the squared
inequality independent of the existence theorem for roots.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and $b_0, \dots, b_{n-1}$ be
reals, and let $p, q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p, q > 1$ and $\frac1p + \frac1q = 1$
be conjugate exponents ([[thm-young-inequality]]). Then

$$\sum_{k<n} |a_k b_k| \;\le\; \Big(\sum_{k<n} |a_k|^{p}\Big)^{1/p}\Big(\sum_{k<n} |b_k|^{q}\Big)^{1/q}.$$

All powers here are rational powers of nonnegative bases
([[def-rational-power]]): the exponents $p, q, 1/p, 1/q$ are positive rationals,
so the supplementary clause $0^{r} = 0$ covers the vanishing bases and no
expression is left undefined. Taking $p = q = 2$ gives
$\sum_{k<n} |a_k b_k| \le \big(\sum_{k<n} a_k^2\big)^{1/2}\big(\sum_{k<n} b_k^2\big)^{1/2}$,
since $x^{1/2} = \sqrt{x}$ and $|a_k|^2 = a_k^2$. That is not literally the root
form of [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], whose left-hand side is
$\big|\sum_{k<n} a_k b_k\big|$: the two are bridged by
$\big|\sum_{k<n} c_k\big| \le \sum_{k<n} |c_k|$
([[lem-triangle-inequality-finite]]), which is the only step needed to get from
the display above to the root form.

derivations.claim: Put $u=\log(8p^{10})\le13\log p$. Since $a\le1$, $192\tau(\sqrt{u/n}+u/n)\le192\tau(\sqrt{13}+13)\sqrt a<4096\tau\sqrt a=\lambda/2$. The failure bound in [F2] is $1/(4p^9)+1/(32p^{18})\le p^{-8}$. Thus an event $G$ has $P^{\otimes n}$-probability at least $1-p^{-8}$, and on it [F3] bounds squared loss by $C(q,\tau)(c^2a^{1-q}+a)$.

Write $U_{ij}=X_{ij}-EX_{ij}$. By [F1] and [F4], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|U_{ij}|^8\le(2\tau)^4\,4!=384\tau^4$. Also, for unit $v$, $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v\le\int_0^\infty e^{-t/(2\tau)}dt=2\tau$; applying [F6] to centered coordinates gives $|\sigma_{jk}|\le2\tau$. The sample-centered diagonal obeys $0\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\le n^{-1}\sum_iU_{ij}^2$. Applying [F7] to the two centered coordinate sample vectors gives $|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^2\le\widehat\sigma^*_{jj}\widehat\sigma^*_{kk}$. Therefore $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4\le\tfrac12 E_{P^{\otimes n}}[(\widehat\sigma^*_{jj})^4+(\widehat\sigma^*_{kk})^4]\le384\tau^4,$$ where the final inequality uses [F8] with $y_i=U_{ij}^2$ (and likewise for $k$). These bounds are independent of the unknown means.

By [F5], $E_{P^{\otimes n}}|\widehat\sigma_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}|^4\le8E_{P^{\otimes n}}(|\widehat\sigma^*_{jk}|^4+|\sigma_{jk}|^4)\le C\tau^4$. For any matrix $A$, [F7] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\le\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2$ by applying finite Cauchy–Schwarz to each row against a unit vector; [F7] also gives $(\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2)^2\le p^2\sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^4$. Thus $E_{P^{\otimes n}}\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4\le C\tau^4p^4$. Applying [F6] to $\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$ and $\mathbf1_{G^c}$ and using step 1.1 gives $$E_{P^{\otimes n}}[\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2;G^c]\le C\tau^2p^2p^{-4}=C\tau^2p^{-2}.$$ Since $p\ge n^\beta$ implies $n\le p^{1/\beta}\le p$ and $1/p\le\log p$, we have $p^{-2}\le\log p/n=a$. Adding the good-event bound proves the claim uniformly over the class.

citations.quote: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $p\ge2$ be an integer, $0\le q<1$, $c_{n,p}\ge0$, and $\tau>0$. For a symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le p}$, write
$$|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(1)}\ge\cdots\ge|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(p-1)}$$
for the magnitudes of the off-diagonal entries in column $j$, arranged in nonincreasing order. Define
$$G_q(c_{n,p})=\left\{\Sigma:\max_{1\le j\le p}\max_{1\le k\le p-1} k|\sigma_{-j,j}|_{(k)}^q\le c_{n,p}\right\}\quad(0<q<1).$$
For $q=0$, define $G_0(c_{n,p})$ to be the symmetric covariance matrices with at most $c_{n,p}$ nonzero off-diagonal entries in each column. The corresponding law class $\mathcal P_q(\tau,c_{n,p})$ consists of iid laws of $X\in\mathbb R^p$ whose covariance lies in $G_q(c_{n,p})$ and which satisfy
$$P(|v^{\mathsf T}(X-\mathbb E X)|>t)\le e^{-t^2/(2\tau)}
$$
for every unit vector $v$ and every $t>0$. This is a clean sub-Gaussian model; it assumes neither coordinate independence nor robustness to contamination.

Let $M\ge2$ be finite, let $P_1,\ldots,P_M$ be sample laws on one
measurable space, and let $t_1,\ldots,t_M$ lie in a metric space
$(\mathcal T,\rho)$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Suppose
$\rho(t_j,t_l)\ge\Delta>0$ whenever $j\ne l$. Let $J$ be uniform on
$[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, with conditional observation law $P_j$ given $J=j$.
For any probability reference law $Q$, define
$$K_Q:=\frac1M\sum_{j=1}^M D(P_j\|Q)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For every randomized estimator kernel from the observation to $\mathcal T$,
with squared metric loss $\rho(a,t_j)^2$, its uniform average risk and its
maximum risk are each at least
$$\frac{\Delta^2}{4} \left(1-\frac{K_Q+\log2}{\log M}\right).$$
The minimax risk over all randomized estimators obeys this bound as well.
When $K_Q=+\infty$, the displayed lower bound is interpreted as $-\infty$
and is vacuous. Logarithms are natural.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces.

If $V=0$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=0.$$

If $V\ne0$ and $s_1$ is the largest singular value of $T$, then

$$\lVert T\rVert=s_1.$$

In the nonzero case, the maximum in
[[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]] is attained at
a right-singular vector for $s_1$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable
statistic, where $\mathcal G$ is a sigma-algebra on the action set
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). Then
$$K_T(x,B):=\delta_{T(x)}(B)=\mathbf 1_B(T(x)),\qquad x\in\mathcal X,\ B\in\mathcal G,$$
is a probability kernel and therefore a deterministic randomized procedure.

Let $p\ge1$ and let $\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1$ be real symmetric positive-definite
$p\times p$ matrices. Under the Gaussian law and directional KL conventions
of [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]],
$$D\bigl(N_p(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_p(0,\Sigma_1)\bigr)=\frac12\left[\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_1^{-1}\Sigma_0)-p+\log\frac{\det\Sigma_1}{\det\Sigma_0}\right].$$

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$ be finite. For each $i\le n$, let
$(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ be a measurable space and let $P_i,Q_i$ be probability
measures on it. On the finite product measurable space set
$$P=\bigotimes_{i=1}^nP_i,\qquad Q=\bigotimes_{i=1}^nQ_i.$$
With the KL convention of [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]],
$$D(P\|Q)=\sum_{i=1}^nD(P_i\|Q_i),$$
where a sum with an infinite term is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: Put $s=\tau/4$ and $\delta=\tfrac12\min\{1,\sqrt{\log(p+1)/n}\}$. Use $p+1$ Gaussian laws $P_0=N(0,sI_p)$ and $P_j=N(0,s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T}))$, $1\le j\le p$. Each covariance has operator norm at most $3\tau/8<\tau$. If $Z$ is standard normal, $P(|Z|>t)=e^{-t^2/2}\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-w^2/2-tw}dw\le e^{-t^2/2}$. Hence every unit-direction projection of these laws obeys the required tail with parameter $\tau$. Their covariance matrices are diagonal, so [F2] puts every law in every class in the statement.

For $j\ge1$, the Gaussian covariance KL formula with $\Sigma_j=s(I_p+\delta e_je_j^{\mathsf T})$ and $\Sigma_0=sI_p$ gives $$D(P_j\|P_0)=\tfrac12(\delta-\log(1+\delta))\le\delta^2/4,$$ where $\delta-\log(1+\delta)=\int_0^\delta t/(1+t)\,dt\le\delta^2/2$. By finite-product KL additivity, $$D(P_j^{\otimes n}\|P_0^{\otimes n})=nD(P_j\|P_0)\le n\delta^2/4\le\log(p+1)/16.$$ The $j=0$ divergence is zero, so the reference-law average KL has the same bound.

Use the full matrix action space $\mathcal T=\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ and set $\rho(A,B)=\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. For a unit vector $v$, rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] gives $\|Av\|_2^2\le\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2=\|A\|_F^2$, so [F4] gives $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F$. Conversely each coordinate unit vector $e_j$ has norm one, so $\|A\|_F^2=\sum_j\|Ae_j\|_2^2\le p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2$. Thus $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_F\le\sqrt p\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The maximum definition also gives homogeneity, symmetry under $A\mapsto-A$, and $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by the Euclidean triangle inequality on each unit vector. If $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=0$, all columns $Ae_j$ vanish, so $A=0$. Hence $\rho$ is a finite metric by [F5]. The two norm inequalities imply each ball for either metric contains a ball for the other about the same center, so their open sets and therefore their Borel sigma-algebras coincide. Under the entry-list identification $\mathbb R^{p\times p}=\mathbb R^{p^2}$ this is exactly the Euclidean Borel action space in the minimax-risk definition. In particular the diagonal embedding $a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a)$ is continuous: its Frobenius difference norm is $\|a-b\|_2$, and its operator difference norm is at most that. All targets in step 1.1 are thus legitimate Borel metric-space points, and every estimator in the minimax definition is measurable into this metric Borel space and induces an admissible deterministic kernel by [F6]. No new choice axiom is used.

For a diagonal matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(a)$ and a unit vector $v$, $\|Dv\|_2^2=\sum_j a_j^2v_j^2\le\max_j|a_j|^2$; equality holds at a coordinate unit vector attaining the finite maximum. Hence $\|D\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_j|a_j|$. A target difference from the base has one diagonal entry $s\delta$; a difference between two nonbase targets has two entries $s\delta,-s\delta$. Every distinct pair therefore has metric separation exactly $s\delta$.

Apply [F3] to these $p+1$ targets, with the base sample law as reference. Its bracket is at least $1-1/16-\log2/\log3>1/4$. Thus the risk is at least $s^2\delta^2/16\ge(\tau^2/1024)\min\{1,\log p/n\}$. These finite experiments are subsets of the full class, so the full minimax risk is no smaller.
