citations.quote: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $T$ be an endomorphism of an $n$-dimensional vector space over $F$. If

$$\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$$

in $F[x]$, then $\det(T)=\prod_{i<n}\lambda_i$. Thus the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $m\ge1$, let U,V be open subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, and let $T:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Borel $h:V\to[0,\infty]$, $\int_V h(y)\,dy=\int_U h(T(x))|\det DT(x)|\,dx$, with equality in $[0,\infty]$ and $0\cdot\infty=0$. This statement concerns Borel h; no completed-measurable substitution is asserted.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define
$D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in
[[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and let $r=dP/dQ$ be a nonnegative
measurable representative of its Radon–Nikodym class. On $\{r=0\}$ set
$\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$, the choice on this set does not affect
$\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. By the
change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
this is equivalently
$$D(P\|Q)=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
where $0\log0:=0$. Interpret the signed integral by the difference of the
nonnegative integrals of its positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). The negative part is finite: for
$0<t\le1$, the derivative of $-t\log t$ is $-\log t-1$, so this function
has maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$; here $e$ is the natural exponential constant
([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]) and the logarithm derivative is
[[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]]. Thus
the $Q$-integral of the negative part of $r\log r$ is at most $1/e$, and the
extended integral is well-defined without
an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

derivations.claim: Let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_p)$ be the independent standard-normal vector in [F1], and put $\phi_p(z)=\prod_{i=1}^p\phi_1(z_i)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}e^{-\|z\|_2^2/2}$. For every Borel rectangle $R=\prod_iB_i$, [F3] gives $\mathbb P(Z\in R)=\prod_i\int_{B_i}\phi_1(t)\,dt$. Tonelli's theorem and the product-Lebesgue identity in [F4] show that this equals $\int_R\phi_p(z)\,dz$. Rectangles generate the Borel sigma-algebra, so measure uniqueness in [F4] proves that $Z$ has density $\phi_p$.

Let $\Sigma$ be positive definite and write $A=\Sigma^{1/2}$ using the real spectral theorem. If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p>0$ are the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$, then $A$ has eigenvalues $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; [F5] gives $\det A=\sqrt{\det\Sigma}>0$. For a Borel set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, apply [F6] to $T=A$ and the nonnegative Borel function $g_E(x)=\mathbf1_E(x)\phi_p(A^{-1}x)|\det A^{-1}|$. This gives $$\mathbb P(AZ\in E)=\int_E\phi_p(A^{-1}x)|\det A^{-1}|\,dx.$$ Because $\|A^{-1}x\|_2^2=x^T\Sigma^{-1}x$ and $|\det A^{-1}|=(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}$, [F1] yields the positive density $$f_\Sigma(x)=(2\pi)^{-p/2}(\det\Sigma)^{-1/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac12x^T\Sigma^{-1}x\right).$$

The two densities in step 2.1 are strictly positive. Their log ratio is $$\log\frac{f_{\Sigma_0}(x)}{f_{\Sigma_1}(x)}=\frac12\log\frac{\det\Sigma_1}{\det\Sigma_0}+\frac12x^T(\Sigma_1^{-1}-\Sigma_0^{-1})x.$$ It is integrable under $N_p(0,\Sigma_0)$ because it is a constant plus a finite quadratic form and [F1] gives finite second moments. Applying [F7] and [F8], $$D\bigl(N_p(0,\Sigma_0)\|N_p(0,\Sigma_1)\bigr)=\frac12\log\frac{\det\Sigma_1}{\det\Sigma_0}+\frac12\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\Sigma_1^{-1}-\Sigma_0^{-1})\Sigma_0\bigr).$$ The trace identity follows by expanding the quadratic form as a finite sum and using $\mathbb E[X_iX_j]=(\Sigma_0)_{ij}$.

Finite trace linearity and $\Sigma_0^{-1}\Sigma_0=I_p$ give $\operatorname{tr}((\Sigma_1^{-1}-\Sigma_0^{-1})\Sigma_0)=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_1^{-1}\Sigma_0)-p$. Substitution into step 3.1 proves the formula.
